course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 2
unit.description: Follow the Spanish, French, Dutch, and British colonies, the regions of British North America, Atlantic trade, slavery, and colonial society from 1607 to 1754.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: The Regions of British Colonies
lesson.summary: How environment, religion, labor, and distance from Britain produced the Chesapeake, New England, middle, and southern plantation colonies and their self-governing institutions.
learningGoals: Explain how tobacco shaped the economy and labor of the Chesapeake and North Carolina.
Compare the economies and societies of New England, the middle colonies, and the plantation colonies.
Explain why colonial governments developed self-governing institutions.
lesson.bigIdea: The British colonies developed distinct regions because of different environments, motives, and labor systems, and distance from Britain let all of them build self-governing institutions.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain how and why environmental and other factors shaped the development of the British colonies. For each region, ask what the land produced, who did the work, and how the colony governed itself.

sections.title: The Chesapeake and North Carolina: tobacco
sections.conceptTitle: The Chesapeake and North Carolina: tobacco

blocks.text: Virginia and Maryland, the Chesapeake colonies, and North Carolina grew prosperous by exporting tobacco. Jamestown struggled until John Rolfe's tobacco found a market in England, after which planters rushed to claim land. Tobacco was labor-intensive, and at first it was grown mainly by white, mostly male indentured servants who signed contracts to work for a set number of years in exchange for passage.

Later, as fewer servants came and planters wanted a permanent workforce, enslaved Africans increasingly replaced indentured servants. Because most of the early migrants were men, the Chesapeake had unequal numbers of men and women and high death rates from disease.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Indentured servitude was not slavery. Servants worked under contract for a limited time, while slavery was permanent and hereditary.

sections.takeaway: Tobacco drove the Chesapeake economy, first with indentured servants and later with enslaved Africans.

sections.title: New England: towns and a mixed economy
sections.conceptTitle: New England: towns and a mixed economy

blocks.text: Puritans settled New England beginning in the 1620s and 1630s, seeking to build religious communities. Colonists settled in small towns and farmed family-sized plots on rocky soil with short growing seasons. They did not grow a single export crop. Instead they built a thriving mixed economy of agriculture, fishing, shipbuilding, lumber, and trade.

Many families migrated together, and the New England population was healthier and more balanced than the Chesapeake's. Town meetings, where male landholders discussed local affairs, shaped local government.

sections.takeaway: New England's Puritan towns and family farms supported a mixed economy of agriculture and commerce.

sections.title: The middle colonies: grain and diversity
sections.conceptTitle: The middle colonies: grain and diversity

blocks.text: New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Delaware had fertile soil and a longer growing season than New England. Their farmers raised cereal crops, especially wheat, and exported grain and flour, which gave the middle colonies a flourishing export economy. William Penn founded Pennsylvania in 1681 as a refuge for Quakers.

Because their land and trade drew migrants from many places, the middle colonies became more diverse than New England or the South. English, Dutch, German, Scots-Irish, and other settlers, with Protestants of many denominations and some Jews and Catholics, lived side by side, which led to greater cultural, ethnic, and religious diversity and tolerance.

sections.takeaway: Grain exports and migration from many places made the middle colonies diverse and relatively tolerant.

sections.title: The southern Atlantic coast and the West Indies: plantations
sections.conceptTitle: The southern Atlantic coast and the West Indies: plantations

blocks.text: South Carolina, Georgia, and the British West Indies had long growing seasons that supported plantation economies based on exporting cash crops. South Carolina planters grew rice and, later, indigo. In the West Indies, planters on islands such as Barbados and Jamaica grew sugar.

These plantations depended on the labor of enslaved Africans, who often made up the majority of the population in these areas. Enslaved people developed their own forms of cultural and religious autonomy, blending African traditions with new surroundings.

sections.takeaway: Long growing seasons produced cash-crop plantations that relied on enslaved Africans, who were often the majority.

sections.title: Self-government at a distance

blocks.text: Distance and Britain's initially lax attention let the colonies create self-governing institutions that were unusually democratic for the era. In Virginia, the House of Burgesses first met in 1619. In New England, power rested in participatory town meetings, whose members elected representatives to colonial legislatures. In the southern colonies, elite planters exercised local authority and also dominated the elected assemblies.

Voting was limited, usually to white men who owned property, but a much larger share of colonists could vote than in Britain. Colonial assemblies gained experience in taxing and spending, which later shaped how colonists reacted to British control.

sections.takeaway: Weak British oversight let colonists build assemblies and town meetings that were unusually democratic for the era.

connections.title: Regions linked by trade
connections.body: The regions were different, but all depended on trade across the Atlantic. Topic 2.4 explains how that trade worked and how Britain tried to control it.
connections.transferQuestion: How did the products of each region fit into the Atlantic economy?
connections.feedback: A strong answer names each region's export, such as tobacco, grain, fish, or sugar, and explains where it was sold and what labor produced it.
